title: Strengthening the Student Toolbox https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1021069.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 16, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises John Dunlosky's practitioner-facing distillation of ten learning strategies, ranked by research-backed effectiveness. Practice testing and distributed practice come out clearly on top for boosting long-term retention; interleaved practice shows real promise; elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are useful but need more research; and popular default strategies, rereading and highlighting, are shown to be relatively ineffective, with summarisation and imagery offering only limited benefit without proper training. Barton draws out Dunlosky's central argument: teacher training programmes rarely teach students, or teachers, how to learn, and textbooks don't cover it either, so schools need to explicitly teach the toolbox rather than assuming it's picked up incidentally. He lists concrete classroom implementations for each top strategy, such as low-stakes quizzes at the start of class, cumulative exams, mixed practice sets, and why questioning, as the practical payoff of the piece.
points: Practice testing and distributed practice are the two clearly highest-value strategies for long-term retention, out of the ten reviewed.
Rereading and highlighting, the strategies students default to most, are shown to be relatively ineffective on their own.
Teacher training programmes typically don't teach students how to learn, and most textbooks don't cover effective learning strategies either — a genuine gap in the system.
Even the most effective strategies only help if students actually use them, so motivating strategy adoption matters as much as identifying the right strategy.
Concrete implementations are given for each top strategy: low-stakes quizzes at lesson starts, cumulative exams, mixed problem sets on worksheets, and why questioning for elaborative interrogation.
quotes: Practice testing and distributed practice emerge as the most beneficial, significantly boosting long-term retention.

Conversely, common strategies like rereading and highlighting prove relatively ineffective, while others, such as summarization and imagery, show limited benefits without proper training or application.
Teachers should prioritize teaching students how to learn, in addition to teaching them subject-matter content.
Teacher training programs should place more emphasis on teaching students how to use effective learning strategies.
Highlighting has not been shown to be helpful and can even lead to worse performance on tests.

Teaching students content may help them succeed in any given class, but teaching them how to guide their learning of content using effective strategies will allow them to successfully learn throughout their lifetime
